nodes.name: First-order black-box optimization method
nodes.statement: According to this model, a \emph{first-order black-box} optimization method is an algorithm which has knowledge of the underlying space $\real^d$ and the family $\mathcal{F}$, the function itself is not known. To gain information on the function to be minimized, the algorithm queries a first order oracle, that is, a subroutine which given as input a point in $\real^d$, returns the value of the objective function and its gradient at that point. The algorithm thus generates a finite sequence of points $\{x_i\in \mathbb{R}^d : i=0,\dots,N\}$, where at each step the algorithm can depend only on the previous steps, their function values and gradients via some rule $$ x_0 \in \real^d,\; x_{i+1}={\cal A}(x_0,\dots,x_i; f(x_0),\dots,f(x_i); f'(x_0),\dots, f'(x_i)), \; i=0, \ldots, N-1, $$ where $f'(\cdot)$ stands for the gradient of $f(\cdot)$.
nodes.statement_short: An algorithm that knows only $\real^d$ and the class $\mathcal{F}$ and accesses $f$ solely through a first-order oracle returning $f(x)$ and $f'(x)$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: $\varepsilon$-optimal solution
nodes.statement: Given a desired accuracy $\varepsilon >0$, applying the given algorithm on the function $f$ in the class $\mathcal{F}$, the algorithm stops when it produces an approximate solution $x_\varepsilon$ which is $\varepsilon$-optimal, that is such that $$f(x_\epsilon) - f(x_\ast) \leq \epsilon.$$
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Absolute inaccuracy $\delta(f,x_N)$
nodes.statement: Equivalently, we can measure the performance of an algorithm by looking at the absolute inaccuracy $$ \delta(f,x_N) = f(x_N) - f(x_\ast),$$ where $x_N$ is the result of the algorithm after making $N$ calls to the oracle.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Notation
nodes.statement: For a differentiable function $f$, its gradient at $x$ is denoted by $f'(x)$. The Euclidean norm of a vector $x\in\real^d$ is denoted as $\|x\|$. The set of symmetric matrices in $\real^{n\times n}$ is denoted by $\mathbb{S}^n$. For two symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$, $A\succeq B, (A \succ B)$ means $A-B \succeq 0 \,(A-B \succ 0)$ is positive semidefinite (positive definite). We use $e_i$ for the $i$-th canonical basis vector in $\mathbb{R}^N$, which consists of all zero components, except for its $i$-th entry which is equal to one, and use $\nu$ to denote a unit vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$. For an optimization problem (P), $\val(P)$ stands for its optimal value.
nodes.statement_short: Fixes $f'(x)$, $\|x\|$, $\mathbb{S}^n$, the Löwner order $\succeq$, the canonical vectors $e_i$, the unit vector $\nu$, and $\val(P)$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Normalized inaccuracies $\delta_i$ and normalized gradients $g_i$
nodes.statement: Now define \begin{align*} \delta_i &:= \frac{1}{L\|x_\ast-x_0\|^2}(f(x_i)-f(x_\ast)),\quad i=0,\dots,N, \ast \\ g_i &:= \frac{1}{L\|x_\ast-x_0\|}f^\prime(x_i),\quad i=0,\dots,N, \ast \end{align*} and note that we always have $\delta_\ast=0$ and $g_\ast=0$.
nodes.statement_short: Scale-free variables $\delta_i$ (function-value gaps) and $g_i$ (gradients), normalized by $L$ and $\|x_\ast-x_0\|$.
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Gradient matrix $G$ and canonical unit vectors $u_i$
nodes.statement: Let $G$ denote the $(N+1)\times d$ matrix whose rows are $g_0^T,\dots g_N^T$, and for notational convenience let $u_i\in\mathbb{R}^{N+1}$ denote the canonical unit vector \[ u_i = e_{i+1}, \quad i=0,\dots,N. \] Then for any $i,j$, we have \[ g_i= G^T u_i,\; \trace (G^T u_i u_j^T G)=\langle g_i, g_j \rangle, \;\mbox{and}\; \langle G^T u_i,\nu \rangle=\langle g_i, \nu\rangle. \]
nodes.statement_short: Stacks the normalized gradients into a matrix $G$ so that inner products become traces $\trace(G^T u_i u_j^T G)$.
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Matrices $A_{i,j}, B_{i,j}, C_i, D_i$
nodes.statement: Therefore, by defining the following $(N+1)\times (N+1)$ symmetric matrices \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} A_{i,j} &= \frac{1}{2} (u_i-u_j)(u_i-u_j)^T + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=i+1}^{j} h (u_j u_{t-1}^T+u_{t-1} u_j^T),\\ B_{i,j} &= \frac{1}{2} (u_i-u_j)(u_i-u_j)^T - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=j+1}^{i} h (u_j u_{t-1}^T+u_{t-1} u_j^T),\\ C_i &= \frac{1}{2} u_i u_i^T,\\ D_i &= \frac{1}{2} u_i u_i^T+ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{i} h (u_i u_{t-1}^T + u_{t-1} u_i^T), \end{aligned} \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The four symmetric data matrices that encode the convexity/smoothness inequalities of the gradient-method PEP as quadratic forms in $G$.
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Matrices $\tilde{A}_{i,j}, \tilde{B}_{i,j}, \tilde{C}_i, \tilde{D}_i$
nodes.statement: where $\tilde{A}_{i,j}$, $\tilde{B}_{i,j}$, $\tilde{C}_i$ and $\tilde{D}_i$ are defined, similarly to \eqref{E:gradientmatrices}, by \begin{equation} \begin{aligned} \tilde{A}_{i,j} &= \frac{1}{2} (u_i-u_j)(u_i-u_j)^T + \frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=i+1}^{j} \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} h_k^{(t)}(u_j u_k^T+u_k u_j^T),\\ \tilde{B}_{i,j} &= \frac{1}{2} (u_i-u_j)(u_i-u_j)^T - \frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=j+1}^{i} \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} h_k^{(t)}(u_j u_k^T+u_k u_j^T),\\ \tilde{C}_i &= \frac{1}{2} u_i u_i^T,\\ \tilde{D}_i &= \frac{1}{2} u_i u_i^T+ \frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{i} \sum_{k=0}^{t-1} h_k^{(t)} (u_i u_k^T + u_k u_i^T) \end{aligned} \end{equation} and we recall that $\nu \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a given unit vector, $u_i=e_{i+1}\in\mathbb{R}^{N+1}$ and the notation $i <j=0,\dots,N$ is a shorthand notation for $i=0,\dots,N-1, j= i+1,\dots, N$.
nodes.statement_short: Generalization of $A,B,C,D$ to the class (FO), with the single step $h$ replaced by the full step-size array $h_k^{(t)}$.
nodes.section: 4.2 A Numerical Bound for FO

nodes.name: Step sizes $h^{(i+1)}_k$ realizing FGM inside the class FO
nodes.statement: \begin{align} h^{(i+1)}_k = \begin{cases} \frac{t_{i}-1}{t_{i+1}}h^{(i)}_k & k+2\leq i, \\ \frac{t_{i}-1}{t_{i+1}}(h^{(i)}_{i-1}-1) & k = i-1, \\ 1+\frac{t_{i}-1}{t_{i+1}} & k = i \end{cases} \qquad (i=1,\dots,N-1, \ k=1,\dots,i). \end{align} and \begin{align*} t_i = \begin{cases} 1 & i=1 \\ \frac{1+\sqrt{1+4 t_{i-1}^2}}{2} & i>1. \end{cases} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Recursive step-size array, driven by Nesterov's $t_i$ sequence, that reproduces the fast gradient method as an instance of (FO).
nodes.section: 4.1 A General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples

nodes.name: Dual feasible set $\tilde{\Lambda}$
nodes.statement: \tilde{\Lambda} = \{ (\lambda,\tau) \in \real^{N}_{+}\times \real^{N+1}_{+} : \tau_0 = \lambda_1, \ \lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}+\tau_i = 0, \ i=1,\dots,N-1,\ \lambda_N+\tau_N=1 \}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The polyhedral set of nonnegative multiplier pairs $(\lambda,\tau)$ linked by the telescoping equalities of the dual of (Q$^\prime$).
nodes.section: 4.2 A Numerical Bound for FO

nodes.name: Linearizing variables $r_{i,k}$
nodes.statement: Introducing the new variables: \begin{equation} r_{i,k}= \lambda_i h_k^{(i)}+\tau_i \sum_{t=k+1}^{i} h_k^{(t)}, \quad i=1,\dots,N,\ k=0,\dots,i-1 \end{equation} and denoting $r=(r_{i,k})_{0\leq k<i \leq N}$
nodes.statement_short: Change of variable absorbing the bilinear products of multipliers and step sizes, turning (BIL) into a linear SDP.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class FO

nodes.name: Matrix family $M_k$
nodes.statement: We begin by deriving a recursion rule for the determinant of matrices of the following form: \[ M_k= \begin{pmatrix} d_0 & a_1 & a_2 & \dots & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_1 & d_1 & a_2 & & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_2 & a_2 & d_2 & & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ \vdots & & & \ddots & & \vdots\\ a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & & d_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_k & a_k & a_k & \dots & a_k & d_k \end{pmatrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: The staircase-symmetric matrix family whose leading principal minors are those of $S_1$.
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma 3.3

nodes.name: Objective is convex and $C^{1,1}_L$
nodes.statement: $f:\real^d \to \real$ is a convex function of the type $C^{1,1}_L(\real^d)$, i.e., continuously differentiable with Lipschitz continuous gradient: \[ \|f'(x)-f'(y)\|\leq L \|x-y\|,\,\,\forall x,y\in \real^d, \] where $L>0$ is the Lipschitz constant.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Problem and Basic Assumptions

nodes.name: Problem (M) is solvable
nodes.statement: We assume that (M) is solvable, i.e., the optimal set $X_*(f):=\Argmin f$ is nonempty, and for $x_*\in X_*(f)$ we set $f^*:=f(x_*).$
nodes.section: 2.1 The Problem and Basic Assumptions

nodes.name: Distance from $x_0$ to the optimal set is bounded by $R$
nodes.statement: There exists $R>0$, such that the distance from $x_0$ to an optimal solution $x_\ast\in X_*(f)$ is bounded by $R$.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Problem and Basic Assumptions

nodes.name: Assumption 1
nodes.statement: {\bf Assumption 1} Problem \eqref{P:foprd} is solvable, i.e., the minimum is finite and attained for the given step-sizes $h^{(i)}_k$.
nodes.statement_short: The dual SDP (DQ$^\prime$) attains a finite minimum for the given step sizes.
nodes.section: 4.2 A Numerical Bound for FO

nodes.name: (M) Unconstrained smooth convex minimization
nodes.statement: (M)\quad \min\{ f(x):\, x \in \real^d\}.
nodes.section: 2.1 The Problem and Basic Assumptions

nodes.name: Performance Estimation Problem (PEP)
nodes.statement: \max \quad & f(x_N)-f(x_\ast) \\ \text{s.t. }\quad & f \in \mathcal{F},\\ & x_{i+1}={\cal A}(x_0,\dots,x_i; f(x_0),\dots,f(x_i); f'(x_0),\dots, f'(x_i)), \; i=0, \ldots, N-1,\\ & x_\ast \in X_\ast(f), \|x_\ast-x_0\|\leq R\\ & x_0, \ldots, x_N, x_\ast \in\mathbb{R}^d. \end{aligned} \tag{P}
nodes.statement_short: Maximize the absolute inaccuracy $f(x_N)-f(x_\ast)$ over all functions in $\mathcal{F}$ and all admissible iterate sequences with $\|x_\ast-x_0\|\leq R$.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: (G) PEP for the gradient method as a quadratic matrix program
nodes.statement: \max_{G\in \mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times d},\delta \in\mathbb{R}^{N+1}}\ & LR^2 \delta_N \\ \text{s.t. } & \trace (G^T A_{i,j} G) \leq \delta_i - \delta_j,\quad i<j=0,\dots,N, \\ & \trace(G^T B_{i,j} G) \leq \delta_i - \delta_j,\quad j<i=0,\dots,N, \\ & \trace(G^T C_i G) \leq \delta_i,\quad i=0,\dots,N, \\ & \trace(G^T D_i G+ \nu u_i^T G ) \leq - \delta_i,\quad i=0,\dots,N. \end{aligned} \tag{G}
nodes.statement_short: The finite-dimensional nonconvex quadratic matrix program whose value upper-bounds the worst-case inaccuracy of (GM).
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: (G$^\prime$) Relaxed PEP for the gradient method
nodes.statement: \max_{G\in \mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times d},\delta \in\mathbb{R}^{N+1}}\ & LR^2 \delta_N \\ \text{s.t. } & \trace (G^T A_{i-1,i} G) \leq \delta_{i-1} - \delta_i,\quad i=1,\dots,N, \\ & \trace(G^T D_i G+ \nu u_i^T G ) \leq - \delta_i,\quad i=0,\dots,N. \end{aligned} \tag{G$^\prime$}
nodes.statement_short: (G) with all constraints discarded except the consecutive-iterate ones and the $x_\ast$ ones.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: (DG$^\prime$) Lagrangian dual of (G$^\prime$)
nodes.statement: \min_{\lambda \in \real^N, t \in \real}\{\frac{1}{2} LR^2 t:\; \lambda \in \Lambda, \; S(\lambda, t) \succeq 0 \}, \end{aligned} \tag{DG$^\prime$}
nodes.statement_short: A small convex program in $(\lambda,t)$ with a single linear-matrix-inequality constraint $S(\lambda,t)\succeq 0$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: (Q) PEP for the class of first-order methods (FO)
nodes.statement: \max_{G\in \mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times d},\delta_i \in\mathbb{R}}\ & LR^2 \delta_N \\ \text{s.t. } & \trace (G^T \tilde{A}_{i,j} G) \leq \delta_i - \delta_j,\quad i<j=0,\dots,N, \\ & \trace(G^T \tilde{B}_{i,j} G) \leq \delta_i - \delta_j,\quad j<i=0,\dots,N, \\ & \trace(G^T \tilde{C}_i G) \leq \delta_i,\quad i=0,\dots,N, \\ & \trace(G^T \tilde{D}_i G+ \nu u_i^T G ) \leq - \delta_i,\quad i=0,\dots,N, \end{aligned} \tag{Q}
nodes.statement_short: The analogue of (G) for the whole class (FO), built from the matrices $\tilde A,\tilde B,\tilde C,\tilde D$.
nodes.section: 4.2 A Numerical Bound for FO

nodes.name: (Q$^\prime$) Relaxed PEP for the class (FO)
nodes.statement: \max_{G\in \mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times d},\delta_i \in\mathbb{R}}\ & LR^2 \delta_N \\ \text{s.t. } & \trace (G^T \tilde{A}_{i-1,i} G) \leq \delta_{i-1} - \delta_i,\quad i=1,\dots,N, \\ & \trace(G^T \tilde{D}_i G+ \nu u_i^T G ) \leq - \delta_i,\quad i=0,\dots,N. \end{aligned} \tag{Q$^\prime$}
nodes.statement_short: (Q) restricted to consecutive-index and $x_\ast$ constraints, mirroring (G$^\prime$).
nodes.section: 4.2 A Numerical Bound for FO

nodes.name: (DQ$^\prime$) Dual semidefinite program of (Q$^\prime$)
nodes.statement: \min_{\lambda, \tau,t}\ & \frac{1}{2} t \\ \text{s.t. } & \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i \tilde{A}_{i-1,i} + \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i \tilde{D}_i &\frac{1}{2} \tau \\ \frac{1}{2} \tau^T & \frac{1}{2} t \end{pmatrix} \succeq 0, \\ & (\lambda, \tau) \in \tilde{\Lambda}, \end{aligned} \tag{DQ$^\prime$}
nodes.statement_short: A convex SDP in $(\lambda,\tau,t)$ whose optimal value times $LR^2$ bounds the performance of any method in (FO).
nodes.section: 4.2 A Numerical Bound for FO

nodes.name: (BIL) Bilinear optimal-step-size problem
nodes.statement: \min_{h,\lambda, \tau,t}\ \left \{ \frac{1}{2} t : \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i \tilde{A}_{i-1,i}(h) + \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i \tilde{D}_i(h) &\frac{1}{2} \tau \\ \frac{1}{2} \tau^T & \frac{1}{2} t \end{pmatrix} \succeq 0, (\lambda, \tau) \in \tilde{\Lambda} \right\}, \end{aligned} \tag{BIL}
nodes.statement_short: Minimize the (DQ$^\prime$) bound jointly over multipliers and over the step sizes $h$ that define the algorithm.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class FO

nodes.name: (LIN) Linear SDP relaxation of (BIL)
nodes.statement: \min_{r,\lambda, \tau,t}\ \left\{ \frac{1}{2} t : \begin{pmatrix} S(r,\lambda,\tau) &\frac{1}{2} \tau \\ \frac{1}{2} \tau^T & \frac{1}{2} t \end{pmatrix} \succeq 0, \ (\lambda, \tau) \in \tilde{\Lambda} \right\}, \end{aligned} \tag{LIN}
nodes.statement_short: (BIL) after the substitution $r_{i,k}$, giving a convex SDP solvable by standard numerical methods.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class FO

nodes.name: Proposition 3.1 (fundamental inequality for convex $C^{1,1}_L$ functions)
nodes.statement: Let $f:\real^d \to \real$ be convex and $C^{1,1}_L$. Then, \begin{equation} \frac{1}{2L} \|f^\prime(x)-f^\prime(y)\|^2 \leq f(x)-f(y)-\langle f^\prime(y), x-y\rangle, \;\mbox{for all} \; x,y\in \mathbb{R}^d. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For convex $L$-smooth $f$, the squared gradient difference is dominated by the Bregman gap: $\frac{1}{2L}\|f'(x)-f'(y)\|^2 \le f(x)-f(y)-\langle f'(y),x-y\rangle$.
nodes.section: 3.1 A Performance Estimation Problem for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Lemma 3.1 (dimension reduction for a quadratic matrix function)
nodes.statement: Let $f(X)=\trace (X^T Q X + 2 ba^T X)$ be a quadratic function, where $X\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$, $Q\in \mathbb{S}^n$, $a\in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $0\neq b\in \mathbb{R}^m$. Then \[ \inf_{X\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}} f(X) = \inf_{\xi\in \mathbb{R}^n} f(\xi b^T). \]
nodes.statement_short: Minimizing $\trace(X^TQX+2ba^TX)$ over all matrices $X$ is the same as minimizing over rank-one matrices $\xi b^T$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method
assumptions: $f(X)=\trace (X^T Q X + 2 ba^T X)$ be a quadratic function, where $X\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}$, $Q\in \mathbb{S}^n$, $a\in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $0\neq b\in \mathbb{R}^m$

nodes.name: Lemma 3.2 (Lagrangian dual of (G$^\prime$))
nodes.statement: Consider problem \eqref{P:gpr} for any fixed $h\in \real$ and $L,R >0$. A Lagrangian dual of \eqref{P:gpr} is given by the following convex program: \begin{align*} \begin{aligned} \min_{\lambda \in \real^N, t \in \real}\{\frac{1}{2} LR^2 t:\; \lambda \in \Lambda, \; S(\lambda, t) \succeq 0 \}, \end{aligned} \tag{DG$^\prime$} \end{align*} where $\Lambda:=\{\lambda \in \real^N:\; \lambda_{i+1}-\lambda_i \geq 0, \quad i=1,\dots,N-1,\; 1-\lambda_N \geq 0,\; \lambda_i \geq 0,\quad i=1,\dots,N\}$, the matrix $S(\cdot,\cdot)\in \mathbb{S}^{N+2}$ is given by \[ S(\lambda,t)=\begin{pmatrix} (1-h)S_0 + h S_1 & q \\ q^T & t \end{pmatrix}, \] with $q=(\lambda_1,\lambda_2-\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1},1-\lambda_N)^T$ and where the matrices $S_0, S_1\in \mathbb{S}^{N+1}$ are defined by: {\small \begin{equation} S_0= \begin{pmatrix} 2 \lambda_1 & -\lambda_1 \\ -\lambda_1 & 2 \lambda_2 & -\lambda_2 \\ & -\lambda_2 & 2 \lambda_3 & -\lambda_3 \\ & & \ddots &\ddots & \ddots\\ & & & -\lambda_{N-1} & 2 \lambda_N & -\lambda_N \\ & & & & -\lambda_N & 1\\ \end{pmatrix} \end{equation} } and {\small {\begin{equation} S_1= \begin{pmatrix} 2 \lambda_1 & \lambda_2-\lambda_1 &\dots &\lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} &1-\lambda_N \\ \lambda_2-\lambda_1 & 2 \lambda_2 & &\lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} &1-\lambda_N \\ \vdots & & \ddots & &\vdots \\ \lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} & \lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} & & 2\lambda_N & 1-\lambda_N \\ 1-\lambda_N & 1-\lambda_N & \dots & 1-\lambda_N & 1 \\ \end{pmatrix} . \end{equation}}}
nodes.statement_short: A Lagrangian dual of (G$^\prime$) is the convex program $\min\{\frac12 LR^2 t: \lambda\in\Lambda,\ S(\lambda,t)\succeq 0\}$ with $S$ built from $S_0,S_1$.

nodes.name: Algorithm GM (gradient method with constant step size)
nodes.statement: {\bf Algorithm GM} \medskip \begin{enumerate} \setcounter{enumi}{-1} \item Input: $f\in C^{1,1}_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$ convex, $x_0\in \mathbb{R}^d.$ \item For $i=0,\dots,N-1$, compute $x_{i+1} = x_i - \frac{h}{L} f^\prime(x_i)$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: The Heavy Ball Method (HBM)
nodes.statement: \textbf{The Heavy Ball Method (HBM)} \fbox{\parbox{14cm}{ {\bf Algorithm HBM} \medskip \begin{enumerate} \setcounter{enumi}{-1} \item Input: $f\in C^{1,1}_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$, $x_0\in \mathbb{R}^d$, \item $x_1 \leftarrow x_0 - \frac{\alpha}{L} f^\prime(x_0)$ \item For $i=1,\dots,N-1$ compute: $x_{i+1} = x_i - \frac{\alpha}{L} f^\prime(x_i) +\beta (x_i-x_{i-1})$ \end{enumerate} }} \medskip Here the step sizes $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are chosen such that $0 \leq \beta < 1$ and $0 < \alpha < 2(1+\beta)$, see \cite{polyak1964}.
nodes.statement_short: Gradient step plus a momentum term $\beta(x_i-x_{i-1})$, with $0\leq\beta<1$ and $0<\alpha<2(1+\beta)$.

nodes.name: The fast gradient method (FGM)
nodes.statement: \textbf{The fast gradient method (FGM)} \fbox{\parbox{14cm}{ {\bf Algorithm FGM} \medskip \begin{enumerate} \setcounter{enumi}{-1} \item Input: $f\in C^{1,1}_L(\mathbb{R}^d)$, $x_0\in \mathbb{R}^d$, \item $y_1 \leftarrow x_0$, $t_1 \leftarrow 1$, \item For $i=1,\dots,N$ compute: \begin{enumerate} \item $x_i \leftarrow y_i -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_i)$, \item $t_{i+1} \leftarrow \frac{1+\sqrt{1+4 t_i^2}}{2}$, \item $y_{i+1} \leftarrow x_i + \frac{t_i-1}{t_{i+1}}(x_i-x_{i-1})$. \end{enumerate} \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Nesterov's accelerated scheme: gradient step on the auxiliary sequence $y_i$ plus extrapolation with weights $\frac{t_i-1}{t_{i+1}}$.

nodes.name: Motivation for deriving an alternative low-dimensional dual
nodes.statement: We are interested in deriving a dual problem for \eqref{P:gpr} which is as simple as possible, especially with respect to its dimension. As noted earlier, problem \eqref{P:gpr} is a nonhomogeneous quadratic matrix program, and a dual problem for \eqref{P:gpr} could be directly obtained by applying the results developed by Beck \cite{beck-qm06}. However, the resulting obtained dual will involve an additional matrix variable $\Phi \in \mathbb{S}^d$, where $d$ can be very large. Instead, here by exploiting the special structure of the second set of nonhomogeneous inequalities given in \eqref{P:gpr}, we derive an alternative dual problem, but with only one additional variable $t \in \real$.
nodes.statement_short: Beck's generic QMP dual would introduce a $d\times d$ matrix variable; exploiting structure gives a dual with one extra scalar $t$.

nodes.statement: First note that both (G) and \eqref{P:gpr} are clearly feasible and $\val (G) \leq\val\eqref{P:gpr}$. Invoking Lemma \ref{lem:dual}, by weak duality for the pair of primal-dual problems \eqref{P:gpr} and \eqref{P:dualgpr}, we thus obtain that $\val\eqref{P:gpr}\leq \val\eqref{P:dualgpr}$ and hence: \begin{equation} f(x_N)-f^* \leq \val (G) \leq \val \eqref{P:gpr} \leq \val \eqref{P:dualgpr}. \end{equation} Now consider the following point $(\lambda,t)$ for the dual problem \eqref{P:dualgpr}: \begin{align*} \lambda_i &= \frac{i}{2 N+1-i},\quad i=1,\dots,N, \\ t &= \frac{1}{2Nh+1}. \end{align*} Assuming that this point is \eqref{P:dualgpr}-feasible, it follows from (\ref{weak}) that $$ f(x_N)-f^* \leq \val\eqref{P:dualgpr} \leq \frac{L R^2}{4 N h+2}, $$ which proves the desired result. Thus, it remains to show that the above given choice $(\lambda, t)$ is feasible for \eqref{P:dualgpr}. First, it is easy to see that all the linear constraints of \eqref{P:dualgpr} on the variables $\lambda_i, i=1,\ldots ,N$ described through the set $\Lambda$ hold true. Now we prove that the matrix $S\equiv S(\lambda,t)$ is positive semidefinite. From Lemma~\ref{L:positivedefinitea0a1}, with $h \in [0,1]$, we get that $(1-h)S_0 + h S_1$ is positive definite, as a convex combination of positive definite matrices. Next, we argue that the determinant of $S$ is zero. Indeed, take $u:=(1,\dots,1,-(2Nh+1))^T$, then from the definition of $S$ and the choice of $\lambda_i$ and $t$ it follows by elementary algebra that $Su=0$. To complete the argument, we note that the determinant of $S$ can also be found via the identity (see, e.g., \cite[Section~A.5.5]{boyd2004}): \[ \det(S) = (t-q^T((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)^{-1}q) \det((1-h)S_0 + h S_1). \] Since we have just shown that $(1-h)S_0 + h S_1 \succ 0$, then $\det((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)>0$ and we get from the above identity that the value of $t-q^T((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)^{-1}q$, which is the Schur complement of the matrix $S$, is equal to 0. By a well known lemma on the Schur complement \cite[Lemma~4.2.1]{ben2001lectures}, we conclude that $S$ is positive semidefinite.
nodes.statement_short: Weak duality plus an explicit dual-feasible point $\lambda_i=i/(2N+1-i)$, $t=1/(2Nh+1)$, whose feasibility follows from Lemma 3.3 and a Schur-complement determinant computation.

First note that the sequence $t_i$ is defined by the two algorithms in the same way. Now let $\{x_i$, $y_i\}$ be the sequences generated by \fastgradalg and denote by $\{y_i^\prime\}$, $x_N^\prime$ the sequence generated by \fastgradalgb. Obviously, $y^\prime_1 = y_1$ and since $t_1=1$ we get using the relations \ref{E:nesterovsteps}: \begin{align*} y_2^\prime &= y_1^\prime - \frac{1}{L} h^{(2)}_1 f^\prime(y_1^\prime) = y_1 - \frac{1}{L} \left(1+\frac{t_{1}-1}{t_2} \right) f^\prime(y_1) = y_1 - \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_1)= x_1 = y_2. \end{align*} Assuming $y_i^\prime = y_i$ for $i = 1,\dots,n$, we then have \begin{align*} y_{n+1}^\prime &= y_n^\prime - \frac{1}{L} h^{(n+1)}_n f^\prime(y_n^\prime) - \frac{1}{L} h^{(n+1)}_{n-1} f^\prime(y_{n-1}^\prime) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} h^{(n+1)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime) \\ &= y_n - \frac{1}{L} (1+\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}) f^\prime(y_n) - \frac{1}{L} \frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}(h^{(n)}_{n-1}-1) f^\prime(y_{n-1}) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} \frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}h^{(n)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime) \\ &= y_n - \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_n) +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} \left( -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_n) + \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_{n-1}) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} h^{(n)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime)\right) \\ &= x_n +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} \left( -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_n) + \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_{n-1}) +y_n^\prime-y_{n-1}^\prime\right) \\ &= x_n +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} (x_n-x_{n-1}) \\ &= y_{n+1}. \end{align*} Finally, \[ x_N^\prime = y_N^\prime -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_N^\prime) = y_N -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_N) = x_N. \]

nodes.statement: As (LIN) is a relaxation of \eqref{P:pblin}, it is enough to show that \eqref{P:pblin} can achieve the same objective value. Let $(r^\ast,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast,t^\ast)$ be an optimal solution for (LIN). If $\lambda_i^\ast \neq 0$ for all $1\leq i \leq N$, then~\eqref{E:solvebil} satisfies all the equations in \eqref{E:definex} and therefore $(h,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast,t^\ast)$ is feasible for \eqref{P:pblin}. Suppose $\lambda^\ast_m=0$ for some $1\leq m \leq N$ and that $m$ is the maximal index with this property. Then by the equality and non-negativity constraints in (LIN), we get that $\lambda^\ast_1=\lambda^\ast_2=\dots=\lambda^\ast_m=0$ and $\tau^\ast_0=\tau^\ast_1=\dots=\tau^\ast_{m-1}=0$. Let $S:=S(r,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast)$, then by the positive semidefinite constraint in (LIN), we have $S \succeq 0$. From the linear equalities connecting $\lambda$ and $\tau$ it follows that \[ S_{i,i}=\begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_1^\ast+\tau_0^\ast) = \lambda_1^\ast, &\quad i=1 \\ \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_i^\ast+\lambda_{i-1}^\ast+\tau_{i-1}^\ast) = \lambda_i^\ast, &\quad i=2,\dots,N \end{cases}, \] and we get that $S_{1,1}=\dots=S_{m,m}=0$. By the properties of positive semidefinite matrices we now get that $r_{i,k}^\ast=0$ for $i=1,\dots,m$ and $k=0,\dots,i-1$, hence the set of equations \eqref{E:definex} with the chosen values of $h_k^{(i)}$ is consistent.

nodes.statement: We now establish the positive definiteness of the matrices $S_0$ and $S_1$ given in \eqref{b0matrix} and \eqref{b1matrix}, respectively. \subsection{$S_0 \succ 0$} We begin by showing that $S_0$ is positive definite. Recall that \[ S_0= \begin{pmatrix} 2 \lambda_1 & -\lambda_1 \\ -\lambda_1 & 2 \lambda_2 & -\lambda_2 \\ & -\lambda_2 & 2 \lambda_3 & -\lambda_3 \\ & & \ddots &\ddots & \ddots\\ & & & -\lambda_{N-1} & 2 \lambda_N & -\lambda_N \\ & & & & -\lambda_N & 1\\ \end{pmatrix} \] for \begin{align*} \lambda_i &= \frac{i}{2 N+1-i}, \qquad i=1,\dots,N. \end{align*} Let us look at $x^T S_0 x$ for any $x=(x_0,\dots,x_N)^T$: \begin{align*} x^T S_0 x &= \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} 2\lambda_{i+1} x_i^2 -2\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \lambda_{i+1} x_i x_{i+1} + x_N^2\\ &= \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \lambda_{i+1} (x_{i+1}-x_i)^2 +\lambda_1 x_0^2+\sum_{i=1}^{N-1} (\lambda_{i+1}-\lambda_i) x_i^2+(1-\lambda_N)x_N^2 \end{align*} which is always positive for $x\neq 0$. We conclude that $S_0$ is positive definite. \subsection{$S_1 \succ 0$} We will show that $S_1$ is positive definite using Sylvester's criterion\footnote{Despite the interesting structure of the matrix $S_1$, this proof is quite involved. A simpler proof would be most welcome!}. Recall that \[ S_1= \begin{pmatrix} 2 \lambda_1 & \lambda_2-\lambda_1 &\dots &\lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} &1-\lambda_N \\ \lambda_2-\lambda_1 & 2 \lambda_2 & &\lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} &1-\lambda_N \\ \vdots & & \ddots & &\vdots \\ \lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} & \lambda_N-\lambda_{N-1} & & 2\lambda_N & 1-\lambda_N \\ 1-\lambda_N & 1-\lambda_N & \dots & 1-\lambda_N & 1 \\ \end{pmatrix} \] for \begin{align*} \lambda_i &= \frac{i}{2 N+1-i}, \qquad i=1,\dots,N. \end{align*} \paragraph{A recursive expression for the determinants} We begin by deriving a recursion rule for the determinant of matrices of the following form: \[ M_k= \begin{pmatrix} d_0 & a_1 & a_2 & \dots & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_1 & d_1 & a_2 & & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_2 & a_2 & d_2 & & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ \vdots & & & \ddots & & \vdots\\ a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & & d_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_k & a_k & a_k & \dots & a_k & d_k \end{pmatrix}. \] To find the determinant of $M_k$, subtract the one before last row multiplied by $\frac{a_{k}}{a_{k-1}}$ from the last row: the last row becomes \[ (0,\dots,0,a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1},d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}). \] Expanding the determinant along the last row we get \[ \det M_k = (d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}) \det M_{k-1}-(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \det (M_k)_{k,k-1} \] where $(M_k)_{k,k-1}$ denotes the $k,k-1$ minor: \[ (M_k)_{k,k-1}= \begin{pmatrix} d_0 & a_1 & a_2 & \dots & a_{k-2} & a_k \\ a_1 & d_1 & a_2 & & a_{k-2} & a_k \\ a_2 & a_2 & d_2 & & a_{k-2} & a_k \\ \vdots & & & \ddots \\ a_{k-2} & a_{k-2} & a_{k-2} & & d_{k-2} & a_k \\ a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & & a_{k-1} & a_k \end{pmatrix} . \] If we multiply the last column of $(M_k)_{k,k-1}$ by $\frac{a_{k-1}}{a_k}$ we get a matrix that is different from $M_{k-1}$ by only the corner element. Thus by basic determinant properties we get that \[ \frac{a_{k-1}}{a_k}\det (M_k)_{k,k-1} = \det M_{k-1}+(a_{k-1}-d_{k-1}) \det M_{k-2}. \] Combining these two results, we have found the following recursion rule for $\det M_k$, $k\geq 2$: \begin{align*} &\det M_k = (d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}) \det M_{k-1} \\&\qquad -(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1})\left(\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}} \det M_{k-1}+(a_{k}-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \det M_{k-2}\right) \\ &= \left((d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k})-(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}\right) \det M_{k-1} -\left(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}\right)^2\det M_{k-2} \end{align*} or \begin{equation} \det M_k= \left(d_k-\frac{2 a_k^2}{a_{k-1}}+\frac{a_k^2 d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}^2} \right) \det M_{k-1}-a_k^2\left(1-\frac{d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}}\right)^2 \det M_{k-2} . \end{equation} Obviously, the recursion base cases are given by \begin{align*} & \det M_0 = d_0, \\ & \det M_1 = d_0 d_1-a_1^2. \end{align*} \paragraph{Closed form expressions for the determinants} Going back to our matrix, $S_1$, by choosing \begin{align*} & d_i = 2\frac{i+1}{2 N-i},\quad i=0,\dots,N-1 \\ & d_N = 1 \\ & a_i = \frac{i+1}{2 N-i}-\frac{i}{2 N+1-i},\quad i=1,\dots,N-1\\ & a_N = 1-\frac{N}{N+1} = \frac{1}{N+1}, \end{align*} we get that $M_k$ is the $k+1$'th leading principal minor of the matrix $S_1$. The recursion rule~\eqref{E:mrecursion} can now be solved for this choice of $a_i$ and $d_i$. The solution is given by: \begin{align} \det M_k =& \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N-k)^2} \left( 1 +\sum_{i=0}^k \frac{2N-2k-1}{2N+4 N i - 2 i^2+1}\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k} \frac{2N+4Ni-2i^2+1}{(2N+1-i)^2}, \end{align} for $k=0,\dots,N-1$, and \begin{align} \det M_N = \det L_1 =& \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2}\prod_{i=0}^{N-1} \frac{2N+4Ni-2i^2+1}{(2N+1-i)^2} . \end{align} \paragraph{Verification} We now proceed to verify the expressions \eqref{E:mkdet} and \eqref{E:mndet} given above. We will show that these expressions satisfy the recursion rule \eqref{E:mrecursion} and the base cases of the problem. We begin by verifying the base cases: \begin{align*} \det M_0 & = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N)^2}\left( 1 +\frac{2N-1}{2N+1}\right) \frac{1}{2N+1}= \frac{1}{N} = d_0, \end{align*} \begin{align*} \det M_1 & = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N-1)^2} \left( 1 +\frac{2N-3}{2N+1}+ \frac{2N-3}{6N -1}\right) \frac{1}{2N+1} \frac{6N-1}{(2N)^2} \\ &= \frac{28N^2-20N-1}{4N^2(2N-1)^2} = \frac{4}{N(2N-1)}-\left(\frac{2}{2N-1}-\frac{1}{2N}\right)^2= d_0 d_1-a_1^2. \end{align*} Now suppose $2 \leq k\leq N$. Denote \begin{align*} \alpha_k &= d_k-\frac{2 a_k^2}{a_{k-1}}+\frac{a_k^2 d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}^2} \\ &=\begin{cases} 4\frac{(2N+1)k-k^2-1}{(2N-k)^2}, &k<N\\ 3\frac{2N^2+2N-1}{(2N+1)^2}, &k=N \end{cases} \\ \beta_k &= a_k^2\left(1-\frac{d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}}\right)^2 \\ &=\begin{cases} \frac{(4 kN-2N-2k^2+4k-1)^2}{(2N-k)^2(2N-k+1)^2}, &k<N\\ \frac{(2N^2+2N-1)^2}{(N+1)^2(2N+1)^2}, &k=N \end{cases}, \end{align*} then the recursion rule \eqref{E:mrecursion} can be written as \begin{align*} & \det M_k= \alpha_k \det M_{k-1} - \beta_k \det M_{k-2}. \end{align*} Further denote \begin{align*} f_i &= \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N-i)^2}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1, \\ g_i &= 2N-2i-1, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1,\\ x_i &= \frac{1}{2N+4 N i - 2 i^2+1}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1, \\ y_i &= \frac{2N+4Ni-2i^2+1}{(2N+1-i)^2}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1, \end{align*} then the solution \eqref{E:mkdet} becomes \begin{align*} \det M_k =& f_k \left(1+g_k \sum_{i=0}^{k} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k} y_i, \end{align*} and \eqref{E:mndet} becomes \begin{align*} \det M_N =& \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2} \prod_{i=0}^{N-1} y_i. \end{align*} Substituting \eqref{E:mkdet} in the RHS of \eqref{E:mrecursion} we get that for $k=2,\dots,N$ \begin{align*} & \alpha_k \det M_{k-1} - \beta_k \det M_{k-2}\\ &= \alpha_k f_{k-1} \left(1+g_{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i - \beta_k f_{k-2}\left(1+g_{k-2}\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i \right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-2} y_i\\ &= \left( \alpha_k f_{k-1} \left(1+g_{k-1} x_{k-1}+g_{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i\right)-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2}-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} g_{k-2}\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i \right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i\\ &= \left( \alpha_k f_{k-1}(1+ g_{k-1} x_{k-1}) -\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2}+\left( \alpha_k f_{k-1} g_{k-1}-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} g_{k-2}\right) \sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i. \end{align*} It is straightforward (although somewhat involved) to verify that for $k<N$ \begin{align*} & \alpha_k f_{k-1} (1+ g_{k-1} x_{k-1}) -\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} = f_k y_k (1+g_k x_{k-1}+g_k x_k), \end{align*} and \begin{align*} & \alpha_k f_{k-1}g_{k-1}-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} g_{k-2} = f_k g_k y_k. \end{align*} We therefore get \begin{align*} & \alpha_k \det M_{k-1} -\beta_k \det M_{k-2} \\ & = \left( f_k y_k(1+g_k x_{k-1}+g_k x_k)+ f_k g_k y_k \sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i\\ & = f_k \left( 1+g_k \sum_{i=0}^{k} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k} y_i\\ & = \det M_k, \end{align*} and thus \eqref{E:mkdet} satisfies \eqref{E:mrecursion}. It is also possible to show that \begin{align*} & \alpha_N f_{N-1}(1+ g_{N-1} x_{N-1}) -\frac{\beta_N}{y_{N-1}} f_{N-2} = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2}, \\ & \alpha_N f_{N-1} g_{N-1}-\frac{\beta_N}{y_{N-1}} f_{N-2} g_{N-2} = 0, \end{align*} thus, for $k=N$ \begin{align*} & \alpha_N \det M_{N-1} -\beta_N \det M_{N-2} \\ & = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2} \prod_{i=0}^{N-1} y_i \\ & = \det M_N, \end{align*} and the expression \eqref{E:mndet} is also verified. \comment{ Mathematica code to verify these statements: \[Lambda][i_] := i/(2 n + 1 - i); a[k_] := (\[Lambda][k + 1] - \[Lambda][k]); d[k_] := 2 \[Lambda][k + 1]; d[n] = 1; a[n] = 1 - \[Lambda][n]; \[Alpha][k_] := (d[k] - (2 a[k]^2)/a[k - 1] + (a[k]^2 d[k - 1])/a[k - 1]^2); \[Beta][k_] := a[k]^2 (1 - d[k - 1]/a[k - 1])^2; f[i_] := (2 n + 1)^2/(2 n - i)^2; g[i_] := 2 n - 2 i - 1; x[i_] := 1/(2 n + 4 n i - 2 i^2 + 1); y[i_] := (2 n + 4 n i - 2 i^2 + 1)/(2 n + 1 - i)^2; Simplify[\[Alpha][k] f[k - 1] (1 + g[k - 1] x[k - 1]) - \[Beta][k]/ y[k - 1] f[k - 2] - f[k] y[k] (1 + g[k] x[k - 1] + g[k] x[k])] Simplify[\[Alpha][k] f[k - 1] g[k - 1] - \[Beta][k]/ y[k - 1] f[k - 2] g[k - 2] - f[k] g[k] y[k]] Simplify[\[Alpha][n] f[n - 1] (1 + g[n - 1] x[n - 1]) - \[Beta][n]/ y[n - 1] f[n - 2] - (2 n + 1)^2/(n + 1)^2] Simplify[\[Alpha][n] f[n - 1] g[n - 1] - \[Beta][n]/ y[n - 1] f[n - 2] g[n - 2]] } To complete the proof, note that the closed form expressions for $\det M_k$ consist of sums and products of positive values, hence $\det M_k$ is positive, and thus follows from Sylvester's criterion that $S_1$ is positive definite.
nodes.statement_short: $S_0 \succ 0$ by completing the square in $x^TS_0x$; $S_1 \succ 0$ by Sylvester's criterion, via a determinant recursion for its leading minors solved in closed form.
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma 3.3

nodes.name: Characterize the matrix minimizer
nodes.statement: First, we recall (this can be easily verified) that $\inf \{f(X): X \in \real^{n\times m}\} >-\infty$ if and only if $Q \succeq 0$, and there exists at least one solution ${\bar X}$ such that \begin{equation} Q{\bar X}+ ab^T=0 \; \Leftrightarrow\; {\bar X}^TQ +ba^T=0, \end{equation} i.e., the above is just $\nabla f (X)= 0$ and characterizes the minimizers of the convex function $f(X)$. Using (\ref{s1}) it follows that $\inf_X f(X)=f({\bar X})=\trace (ba^T{\bar X})$.
nodes.statement_short: Note $\inf f>-\infty$ iff $Q\succeq 0$ with a stationary $\bar X$, and evaluate $\inf_X f=\trace(ba^T\bar X)$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Evaluate the infimum on the rank-one slice
nodes.statement: Now, for any $\xi \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we have $f(\xi b^T)=\|b\|^2(\xi^TQ\xi + 2a^T\xi)$. Thus, likewise, $\inf\{f(\xi b^T): \xi \in \real^n\} >-\infty$ if and only if $Q \succeq 0$ and there exists ${\bar \xi}\in \real^n$ such that \begin{equation} Q{\bar \xi} + a=0,\end{equation} and using (\ref{s2}) it follows $\inf_\xi f(\xi b^T)=f({\bar \xi}b^T)=\|b\|^2a^T{\bar \xi}=\trace (ba^T{\bar \xi}b^T)$.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict to $X=\xi b^T$ and get the analogous stationarity condition $Q\bar\xi+a=0$ and value.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Show the two infima coincide
nodes.statement: Now, using (\ref{s1})-(\ref{s2}), one obtains ${\bar X}^TQ=-ba^T$ and $Q({\bar X}- {\bar \xi}b^T)=0$, and hence it follows that \begin{eqnarray*} f({\bar X})-f({\bar \xi})&=&\trace (ba^T({\bar X}- {\bar \xi}b^T))\\ &=&\trace (-{\bar X}^TQ({\bar X}- {\bar \xi}b^T)=0. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Subtract the two values and use $Q(\bar X-\bar\xi b^T)=0$ to conclude the difference is zero.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Recast (G$^\prime$) as the minimization problem (G$^{\prime\prime}$)
nodes.statement: For convenience, we recast \eqref{P:gpr} as a minimization problem, and we also omit the fixed term $LR^2$ from the objective. That is, we consider the equivalent problem \eqref{P:agpr} defined by \begin{align*} \begin{aligned} \min_{G\in \mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times d},\delta \in\mathbb{R}^{N+1}}\ & -\delta_N \\ \text{s.t. } & \trace (G^T A_{i-1,i} G) \leq \delta_{i-1} - \delta_i,\quad i=1,\dots,N, \\ & \trace(G^T D_i G+ \nu u_i^T G ) \leq - \delta_i,\quad i=0,\dots,N. \end{aligned} \tag{G$^{\prime\prime}$}
nodes.statement_short: Flip the sign of the objective and drop the constant $LR^2$ to get an equivalent minimization problem.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Form the Lagrangian and separate it
nodes.statement: Attaching the dual multipliers $\lambda=(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_N) \in \real^N_{+}$ and $\tau:=(\tau_0, \ldots ,\tau_N)^T \in \real^{N+1}_{+}$ to the first and second set of inequalities respectively, and using the notation $\delta=(\delta_0, \ldots ,\delta_N)$, we get that the Lagrangian of this problem is given as a sum of two separable functions in the variables $(\delta, G)$: \begin{eqnarray*} L(G,\delta, \lambda, \tau)&=& -\delta_N+\sum_{i=1}^{N} \lambda_i(\delta_i - \delta_{i-1}) + \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i \delta_i \\ & &+ \sum_{i=1}^{N} \lambda_i \trace(G^T A_{i-1,i} G)+ \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i \left( \trace(G^T D_i G+ \nu u_i^T G) \right)\\ & \equiv & L_1(\delta, \lambda, \tau)+ L_2(G,\lambda, \tau). \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Introduce multipliers $\lambda,\tau$ and split the Lagrangian into a $\delta$-part $L_1$ and a $G$-part $L_2$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Define the dual objective and the dual problem
nodes.statement: The dual objective function is then defined by $$H(\lambda, \tau)=\min_{G, \delta} L(G,\delta, \lambda\, \tau)=\min_\delta L_1(\delta, \lambda, \tau)+ \min_{G} L_2(G, \lambda, \tau),$$ and the dual problem of \eqref{P:agpr} is then given by \begin{align*} \begin{aligned} \max \{ H(\lambda, \tau):\; \lambda \in\real^{N}_{+}, \tau \in \real^{N+1}_{+}\}. \end{aligned} \tag{DG$^{\prime\prime}$}
nodes.statement_short: Set $H(\lambda,\tau)=\min_\delta L_1+\min_G L_2$ and write the dual (DG$^{\prime\prime}$).
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Eliminate the linear part in $\delta$
nodes.statement: Since $L_1(\cdot,\lambda, \tau)$ is linear in $\delta$, we have $\min_\delta L_1(\delta,\lambda, \tau) =0$ whenever \begin{eqnarray} -\lambda_1 +\tau_0 &= & 0, \nonumber\\ \lambda_i-\lambda_{i+1}+\tau_i &=& 0\quad (i=1,\dots,N-1), \\ -1+\lambda_N+\tau_N &=& 0, \nonumber \end{eqnarray} and $-\infty$ otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: Linearity in $\delta$ forces the multiplier equalities (\ref{eqtau}); otherwise the dual value is $-\infty$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Reduce the quadratic part via Lemma 3.1 and the S-lemma
nodes.statement: Invoking Lemma~\ref{L:quadlemma}, we get \begin{align*} \min_{G\in\mathbb{R}^{(N+1)\times d}} L_2(G,\lambda, \tau) = \min_{w\in\mathbb{R}^{N+1}} L_2(w \nu^T,\lambda, \tau). \end{align*} Therefore for any $(\lambda,\tau)$ satisfying (\ref{eqtau}), we have obtained that the dual objective reduces to \begin{eqnarray*} H(\lambda, \tau) &=& \min_{w \in \real^{N+1}}\{w^T \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i A_{i-1,i} + \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i D_i \right) w + \tau^T w \}\\ &=& \max_{t\in \mathbb{R}} \{-\frac{1}{2}t : w^T \left(\sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i A_{i-1,i} + \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i D_i \right) w + \tau^T w \leq -\frac{1}{2}t,\ \forall w\in \mathbb{R}^{N+1} \}\\ &=& \max_{t\in \mathbb{R}} \left\{ -\frac{1}{2}t: \begin{pmatrix} \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i A_{i-1,i} + \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i D_i & \frac{1}{2} \tau \\ \frac{1}{2}\tau^T & \frac{1}{2}t \end{pmatrix} \succeq 0 \right\}. \end{eqnarray*} where the last equality follows from the well known lemma \cite[Page~163]{ben2001lectures}\footnote{Let $M$ be a symmetric matrix. Then, $x^TMx + 2 b^Tx+ c \geq 0, \forall x \in \real^d$ if and only if the matrix $\begin{pmatrix} M & b\\ b^T & c \end{pmatrix}$ is positive semidefinite.}.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.1 collapses $\min_G L_2$ to a vector problem, then the S-lemma turns it into an LMI in $t$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Compute the multiplier-weighted matrix sums
nodes.statement: Now, recalling the definition of the matrices $A_{i-1,i}, D_i$ (see (\ref{E:gradientmatrices})), we obtain {\small \[ \sum_{i=1}^N \lambda_i A_{i-1,i} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix} \lambda_1 & (h-1)\lambda_1 \\ (h-1)\lambda_1 & \lambda_1+\lambda_2 & (h-1)\lambda_2 \\ & (h-1)\lambda_2 & \lambda_2 +\lambda_3 & (h-1)\lambda_3 \\ & & \ddots &\ddots & \ddots\\ & & & (h-1)\lambda_{N-1} & \lambda_{N-1}+ \lambda_N & (h-1)\lambda_N \\ & & & & (h-1)\lambda_N & \lambda_N\\ \end{pmatrix} \] } and {\small \[ \sum_{i=0}^N \tau_i D_i = \frac{1}{2} \begin{pmatrix} \tau_0 & h\tau_1 & \dots &h\tau_{N-1} &h\tau_N \\ h\tau_1 & \tau_1 & &h\tau_{N-1} &h\tau_N \\ \vdots & & \ddots & &\vdots \\ h\tau_{N-1} & h\tau_{N-1} & & \tau_{N-1} & h\tau_N \\ h\tau_N & h\tau_N & \dots & h\tau_N & \tau_N \\ \end{pmatrix}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Write $\sum\lambda_i A_{i-1,i}$ and $\sum\tau_i D_i$ explicitly as tridiagonal and full matrices.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Eliminate $\tau$ and obtain the stated dual
nodes.statement: Finally, using the relations (\ref{eqtau}) to eliminate $\tau_i$, and recalling that $\val\!\eqref{P:agpr}$ was defined as $-LR^2 \val\!\eqref{P:gpr}$, the desired form of the stated dual problem follows.
nodes.statement_short: Substituting $\tau$ out yields exactly $S(\lambda,t)=(1-h)S_0+hS_1$ and the claimed dual (DG$^\prime$).
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Chain of weak-duality inequalities
nodes.statement: First note that both (G) and \eqref{P:gpr} are clearly feasible and $\val (G) \leq\val\eqref{P:gpr}$. Invoking Lemma \ref{lem:dual}, by weak duality for the pair of primal-dual problems \eqref{P:gpr} and \eqref{P:dualgpr}, we thus obtain that $\val\eqref{P:gpr}\leq \val\eqref{P:dualgpr}$ and hence: \begin{equation} f(x_N)-f^* \leq \val (G) \leq \val \eqref{P:gpr} \leq \val \eqref{P:dualgpr}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Feasibility plus weak duality give $f(x_N)-f^*\leq\val(G)\leq\val(G^\prime)\leq\val(DG^\prime)$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Exhibit the candidate dual point
nodes.statement: Now consider the following point $(\lambda,t)$ for the dual problem \eqref{P:dualgpr}: \begin{align*} \lambda_i &= \frac{i}{2 N+1-i},\quad i=1,\dots,N, \\ t &= \frac{1}{2Nh+1}. \end{align*} Assuming that this point is \eqref{P:dualgpr}-feasible, it follows from (\ref{weak}) that $$ f(x_N)-f^* \leq \val\eqref{P:dualgpr} \leq \frac{L R^2}{4 N h+2}, $$ which proves the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Plug in $\lambda_i=i/(2N+1-i)$ and $t=1/(2Nh+1)$ to get the bound $LR^2/(4Nh+2)$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Check the linear dual constraints
nodes.statement: Thus, it remains to show that the above given choice $(\lambda, t)$ is feasible for \eqref{P:dualgpr}. First, it is easy to see that all the linear constraints of \eqref{P:dualgpr} on the variables $\lambda_i, i=1,\ldots ,N$ described through the set $\Lambda$ hold true.
nodes.statement_short: The chosen $\lambda$ trivially satisfies the monotonicity and sign constraints defining $\Lambda$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Positive definiteness of $(1-h)S_0+hS_1$
nodes.statement: Now we prove that the matrix $S\equiv S(\lambda,t)$ is positive semidefinite. From Lemma~\ref{L:positivedefinitea0a1}, with $h \in [0,1]$, we get that $(1-h)S_0 + h S_1$ is positive definite, as a convex combination of positive definite matrices.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.3 makes $S_0,S_1\succ 0$, so their convex combination is positive definite for $h\in[0,1]$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: The determinant of $S$ vanishes
nodes.statement: Next, we argue that the determinant of $S$ is zero. Indeed, take $u:=(1,\dots,1,-(2Nh+1))^T$, then from the definition of $S$ and the choice of $\lambda_i$ and $t$ it follows by elementary algebra that $Su=0$.
nodes.statement_short: The explicit vector $u=(1,\dots,1,-(2Nh+1))^T$ is in the kernel of $S$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Conclude $S\succeq 0$ via the Schur complement
nodes.statement: To complete the argument, we note that the determinant of $S$ can also be found via the identity (see, e.g., \cite[Section~A.5.5]{boyd2004}): \[ \det(S) = (t-q^T((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)^{-1}q) \det((1-h)S_0 + h S_1). \] Since we have just shown that $(1-h)S_0 + h S_1 \succ 0$, then $\det((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)>0$ and we get from the above identity that the value of $t-q^T((1-h)S_0 + h S_1)^{-1}q$, which is the Schur complement of the matrix $S$, is equal to 0. By a well known lemma on the Schur complement \cite[Lemma~4.2.1]{ben2001lectures}, we conclude that $S$ is positive semidefinite.
nodes.statement_short: The Schur complement of $S$ must therefore be $0$, so $S\succeq 0$ and the dual point is feasible.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Normalization to $L=R=1$
nodes.statement: We will describe two functions that attain the two parts of the $\max$ expression in the above claimed statement. For the sake of simplicity we will assume that $L=1$ and $R=\|x_\ast-x_0\|=1$. Generalizing this proof to general values of $L$ and $R$ can be done by an appropriate scaling.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $L=1$ and $\|x_\ast-x_0\|=1$ by scaling.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: First branch: the Moreau envelope of a norm
nodes.statement:
To show the first part of the $\max$ expression, consider the function \[ \varphi_1(x) =  egin{cases}  rac{1}{2Nh+1} \|x\| - rac{1}{2(2Nh+1)^2} & \| x \| \geq  rac{1}{2Nh+1} \  rac{1}{2} \|x\|^2 & \| x\| <  rac{1}{2Nh+1} \end{cases}. \] Note that this function is nothing else but the Moreau proximal envelope of the function $ rac{1}{2Nh+1}\|x\|$, \cite{M65}. It is well known that this function is convex, continuously differentiable with Lipschitz constant $L=1$, and that its minimal value $\varphi(x_*)=0$, see e.g., \cite{M65, rock-wets-book98}. Applying the gradient method on $\varphi_1(x)$ with $x_0=
u$ where, as before, $
u$ is a unit vector in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we obtain that for $i=0,\dots,N$:  egin{eqnarray*} \varphi_1^\prime(x_i) &=&  rac{1}{2N h+1}
u;\; x_i = \left(1- rac{i h}{2N h+1}ight)
u,\ \mbox{and}\; \varphi_1(x_i) &=&  rac{1}{2N h+1}\left(1- rac{h i}{2N h+1} ight)- rac{1}{2(2N h+1)^2}\ &=&  rac{1}{4Nh+2} \left( rac{4Nh+1-2hi}{2Nh+1}ight). \end{eqnarray*} Therefore, \[ \varphi_1(x_N)-\varphi_1(x_\ast) = \varphi_1(x_N) =  rac{1}{4 N h+2}. \]
nodes.statement_short: The Huber-type function $\varphi_1$ makes the gradient method stall at inaccuracy exactly $1/(4Nh+2)$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: Second branch: the quadratic
nodes.statement: To show the second part of the $\max$ expression, we apply the gradient method on \[ \varphi_2(x) = \frac{1}{2} \|x\|^2 \] with $x_0=\nu$. We then get that for $i=0,\dots,N$: $$ \varphi_2^\prime(x_i)= x_i;\; x_i =(1-h)^i \nu;\; \varphi_2(x_i) = \frac{1}{2}(1-h)^{2i}, $$ and hence \[ \varphi_2(x_N)-\varphi_2(x_\ast) = \varphi_2(x_N) = \frac{1}{2} (1-h)^{2N} \] and the desired claim is proven.
nodes.statement_short: On $\varphi_2(x)=\frac12\|x\|^2$ the iterates contract by $(1-h)$, giving inaccuracy $\frac12(1-h)^{2N}$.
nodes.section: 3.2 A Tight Performance Estimate for the Gradient Method

nodes.name: State the induction claim
nodes.statement: We will show by induction that the sequence $y_i$ generated by Algorithm~\fastgradalgb is identical to the sequence $y_i$ generated by Algorithm~\fastgradalg, and that the value of $x_N$ generated by Algorithm~\fastgradalgb is equal to the value of $x_N$ generated by Algorithm~\fastgradalg.
nodes.statement_short: Induct on $i$ to match the auxiliary sequences of FGM$^\prime$ and FGM, then match $x_N$.
nodes.section: 4.1 A General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples

nodes.name: Base case $i=1,2$
nodes.statement: First note that the sequence $t_i$ is defined by the two algorithms in the same way. Now let $\{x_i$, $y_i\}$ be the sequences generated by \fastgradalg and denote by $\{y_i^\prime\}$, $x_N^\prime$ the sequence generated by \fastgradalgb. Obviously, $y^\prime_1 = y_1$ and since $t_1=1$ we get using the relations \ref{E:nesterovsteps}: \begin{align*} y_2^\prime &= y_1^\prime - \frac{1}{L} h^{(2)}_1 f^\prime(y_1^\prime) = y_1 - \frac{1}{L} \left(1+\frac{t_{1}-1}{t_2} \right) f^\prime(y_1) = y_1 - \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_1)= x_1 = y_2. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Since $t_1=1$, the single step size $h^{(2)}_1$ equals $1$ and $y_2^\prime=y_2$.
nodes.section: 4.1 A General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Assuming $y_i^\prime = y_i$ for $i = 1,\dots,n$, we then have \begin{align*} y_{n+1}^\prime &= y_n^\prime - \frac{1}{L} h^{(n+1)}_n f^\prime(y_n^\prime) - \frac{1}{L} h^{(n+1)}_{n-1} f^\prime(y_{n-1}^\prime) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} h^{(n+1)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime) \\ &= y_n - \frac{1}{L} (1+\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}) f^\prime(y_n) - \frac{1}{L} \frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}(h^{(n)}_{n-1}-1) f^\prime(y_{n-1}) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-2} \frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}h^{(n)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime) \\ &= y_n - \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_n) +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} \left( -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_n) + \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_{n-1}) - \frac{1}{L} \sum_{k=1}^{n-1} h^{(n)}_k f^\prime(y_k^\prime)\right) \\ &= x_n +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} \left( -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_n) + \frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_{n-1}) +y_n^\prime-y_{n-1}^\prime\right) \\ &= x_n +\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}} (x_n-x_{n-1}) \\ &= y_{n+1}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Regroup the gradient sum using the recursion for $h^{(n+1)}_k$ to recover the extrapolation $x_n+\frac{t_n-1}{t_{n+1}}(x_n-x_{n-1})$.
nodes.section: 4.1 A General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples

nodes.name: Match the final iterate $x_N$
nodes.statement: Finally, \[ x_N^\prime = y_N^\prime -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_N^\prime) = y_N -\frac{1}{L} f^\prime(y_N) = x_N. \]
nodes.statement_short: The last line of FGM$^\prime$ reproduces the FGM output $x_N$.
nodes.section: 4.1 A General First-Order Algorithm: Definition and Examples

nodes.name: Reduce to matching objective values
nodes.statement: As (LIN) is a relaxation of \eqref{P:pblin}, it is enough to show that \eqref{P:pblin} can achieve the same objective value. Let $(r^\ast,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast,t^\ast)$ be an optimal solution for (LIN).
nodes.statement_short: Since (LIN) relaxes (BIL), it suffices to realize the same objective value in (BIL).
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class FO

nodes.name: Case all $\lambda_i^\ast \neq 0$
nodes.statement: If $\lambda_i^\ast \neq 0$ for all $1\leq i \leq N$, then~\eqref{E:solvebil} satisfies all the equations in \eqref{E:definex} and therefore $(h,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast,t^\ast)$ is feasible for \eqref{P:pblin}.
nodes.statement_short: The recursion inverts the definition of $r_{i,k}$ exactly, so the recovered $h$ is feasible.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class FO

nodes.name: Case some $\lambda_m^\ast = 0$
nodes.statement: Suppose $\lambda^\ast_m=0$ for some $1\leq m \leq N$ and that $m$ is the maximal index with this property. Then by the equality and non-negativity constraints in (LIN), we get that $\lambda^\ast_1=\lambda^\ast_2=\dots=\lambda^\ast_m=0$ and $\tau^\ast_0=\tau^\ast_1=\dots=\tau^\ast_{m-1}=0$. Let $S:=S(r,\lambda^\ast,\tau^\ast)$, then by the positive semidefinite constraint in (LIN), we have $S \succeq 0$. From the linear equalities connecting $\lambda$ and $\tau$ it follows that \[ S_{i,i}=\begin{cases} \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_1^\ast+\tau_0^\ast) = \lambda_1^\ast, &\quad i=1 \\ \frac{1}{2} (\lambda_i^\ast+\lambda_{i-1}^\ast+\tau_{i-1}^\ast) = \lambda_i^\ast, &\quad i=2,\dots,N \end{cases}, \] and we get that $S_{1,1}=\dots=S_{m,m}=0$. By the properties of positive semidefinite matrices we now get that $r_{i,k}^\ast=0$ for $i=1,\dots,m$ and $k=0,\dots,i-1$, hence the set of equations \eqref{E:definex} with the chosen values of $h_k^{(i)}$ is consistent.
nodes.statement_short: Vanishing diagonal entries of the PSD matrix $S$ force $r^\ast_{i,k}=0$, so setting $h^{(i)}_k=0$ stays consistent.
nodes.section: 5 A Best Performing Algorithm: Optimal Step Sizes for The Algorithm Class FO

nodes.name: $S_0 \succ 0$ by completing the square
nodes.statement: We begin by showing that $S_0$ is positive definite. Recall that \[ S_0= \begin{pmatrix} 2 \lambda_1 & -\lambda_1 \\ -\lambda_1 & 2 \lambda_2 & -\lambda_2 \\ & -\lambda_2 & 2 \lambda_3 & -\lambda_3 \\ & & \ddots &\ddots & \ddots\\ & & & -\lambda_{N-1} & 2 \lambda_N & -\lambda_N \\ & & & & -\lambda_N & 1\\ \end{pmatrix} \] for \begin{align*} \lambda_i &= \frac{i}{2 N+1-i}, \qquad i=1,\dots,N. \end{align*} Let us look at $x^T S_0 x$ for any $x=(x_0,\dots,x_N)^T$: \begin{align*} x^T S_0 x &= \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} 2\lambda_{i+1} x_i^2 -2\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \lambda_{i+1} x_i x_{i+1} + x_N^2\\ &= \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \lambda_{i+1} (x_{i+1}-x_i)^2 +\lambda_1 x_0^2+\sum_{i=1}^{N-1} (\lambda_{i+1}-\lambda_i) x_i^2+(1-\lambda_N)x_N^2 \end{align*} which is always positive for $x\neq 0$. We conclude that $S_0$ is positive definite.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $x^TS_0x$ as a sum of squares with positive coefficients using monotonicity of $\lambda_i$.
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma 3.3

nodes.name: Set up Sylvester's criterion for $S_1$
nodes.statement: We will show that $S_1$ is positive definite using Sylvester's criterion\footnote{Despite the interesting structure of the matrix $S_1$, this proof is quite involved. A simpler proof would be most welcome!}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce $S_1\succ 0$ to positivity of all leading principal minors.
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma 3.3

nodes.name: Determinant recursion for the minors
nodes.statement: We begin by deriving a recursion rule for the determinant of matrices of the following form: \[ M_k= \begin{pmatrix} d_0 & a_1 & a_2 & \dots & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_1 & d_1 & a_2 & & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_2 & a_2 & d_2 & & a_{k-1} & a_k \\ \vdots & & & \ddots & & \vdots\\ a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & & d_{k-1} & a_k \\ a_k & a_k & a_k & \dots & a_k & d_k \end{pmatrix}. \] To find the determinant of $M_k$, subtract the one before last row multiplied by $\frac{a_{k}}{a_{k-1}}$ from the last row: the last row becomes \[ (0,\dots,0,a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1},d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}). \] Expanding the determinant along the last row we get \[ \det M_k = (d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}) \det M_{k-1}-(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \det (M_k)_{k,k-1} \] where $(M_k)_{k,k-1}$ denotes the $k,k-1$ minor: \[ (M_k)_{k,k-1}= \begin{pmatrix} d_0 & a_1 & a_2 & \dots & a_{k-2} & a_k \\ a_1 & d_1 & a_2 & & a_{k-2} & a_k \\ a_2 & a_2 & d_2 & & a_{k-2} & a_k \\ \vdots & & & \ddots \\ a_{k-2} & a_{k-2} & a_{k-2} & & d_{k-2} & a_k \\ a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & a_{k-1} & & a_{k-1} & a_k \end{pmatrix} . \] If we multiply the last column of $(M_k)_{k,k-1}$ by $\frac{a_{k-1}}{a_k}$ we get a matrix that is different from $M_{k-1}$ by only the corner element. Thus by basic determinant properties we get that \[ \frac{a_{k-1}}{a_k}\det (M_k)_{k,k-1} = \det M_{k-1}+(a_{k-1}-d_{k-1}) \det M_{k-2}. \] Combining these two results, we have found the following recursion rule for $\det M_k$, $k\geq 2$: \begin{align*} &\det M_k = (d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k}) \det M_{k-1} \\&\qquad -(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1})\left(\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}} \det M_{k-1}+(a_{k}-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \det M_{k-2}\right) \\ &= \left((d_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}a_{k})-(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}) \frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}\right) \det M_{k-1} -\left(a_k-\frac{a_k}{a_{k-1}}d_{k-1}\right)^2\det M_{k-2} \end{align*} or \begin{equation} \det M_k= \left(d_k-\frac{2 a_k^2}{a_{k-1}}+\frac{a_k^2 d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}^2} \right) \det M_{k-1}-a_k^2\left(1-\frac{d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}}\right)^2 \det M_{k-2} . \end{equation} Obviously, the recursion base cases are given by \begin{align*} & \det M_0 = d_0, \\ & \det M_1 = d_0 d_1-a_1^2. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Row reduction and cofactor expansion give a three-term recursion for $\det M_k$ with base cases $d_0$ and $d_0d_1-a_1^2$.
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma 3.3

nodes.name: Closed-form solution of the recursion
nodes.statement: Going back to our matrix, $S_1$, by choosing \begin{align*} & d_i = 2\frac{i+1}{2 N-i},\quad i=0,\dots,N-1 \\ & d_N = 1 \\ & a_i = \frac{i+1}{2 N-i}-\frac{i}{2 N+1-i},\quad i=1,\dots,N-1\\ & a_N = 1-\frac{N}{N+1} = \frac{1}{N+1}, \end{align*} we get that $M_k$ is the $k+1$'th leading principal minor of the matrix $S_1$. The recursion rule~\eqref{E:mrecursion} can now be solved for this choice of $a_i$ and $d_i$. The solution is given by: \begin{align} \det M_k =& \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N-k)^2} \left( 1 +\sum_{i=0}^k \frac{2N-2k-1}{2N+4 N i - 2 i^2+1}\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k} \frac{2N+4Ni-2i^2+1}{(2N+1-i)^2}, \end{align} for $k=0,\dots,N-1$, and \begin{align} \det M_N = \det L_1 =& \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2}\prod_{i=0}^{N-1} \frac{2N+4Ni-2i^2+1}{(2N+1-i)^2} . \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Specialize $a_i,d_i$ to $S_1$ and state closed-form products for $\det M_k$ and $\det M_N$.
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma 3.3

nodes.name: Verification of the closed forms
nodes.statement: We now proceed to verify the expressions \eqref{E:mkdet} and \eqref{E:mndet} given above. We will show that these expressions satisfy the recursion rule \eqref{E:mrecursion} and the base cases of the problem. We begin by verifying the base cases: \begin{align*} \det M_0 & = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N)^2}\left( 1 +\frac{2N-1}{2N+1}\right) \frac{1}{2N+1}= \frac{1}{N} = d_0, \end{align*} \begin{align*} \det M_1 & = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N-1)^2} \left( 1 +\frac{2N-3}{2N+1}+ \frac{2N-3}{6N -1}\right) \frac{1}{2N+1} \frac{6N-1}{(2N)^2} \\ &= \frac{28N^2-20N-1}{4N^2(2N-1)^2} = \frac{4}{N(2N-1)}-\left(\frac{2}{2N-1}-\frac{1}{2N}\right)^2= d_0 d_1-a_1^2. \end{align*} Now suppose $2 \leq k\leq N$. Denote \begin{align*} \alpha_k &= d_k-\frac{2 a_k^2}{a_{k-1}}+\frac{a_k^2 d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}^2} \\ &=\begin{cases} 4\frac{(2N+1)k-k^2-1}{(2N-k)^2}, &k<N\\ 3\frac{2N^2+2N-1}{(2N+1)^2}, &k=N \end{cases} \\ \beta_k &= a_k^2\left(1-\frac{d_{k-1}}{a_{k-1}}\right)^2 \\ &=\begin{cases} \frac{(4 kN-2N-2k^2+4k-1)^2}{(2N-k)^2(2N-k+1)^2}, &k<N\\ \frac{(2N^2+2N-1)^2}{(N+1)^2(2N+1)^2}, &k=N \end{cases}, \end{align*} then the recursion rule \eqref{E:mrecursion} can be written as \begin{align*} & \det M_k= \alpha_k \det M_{k-1} - \beta_k \det M_{k-2}. \end{align*} Further denote \begin{align*} f_i &= \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(2N-i)^2}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1, \\ g_i &= 2N-2i-1, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1,\\ x_i &= \frac{1}{2N+4 N i - 2 i^2+1}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1, \\ y_i &= \frac{2N+4Ni-2i^2+1}{(2N+1-i)^2}, \quad i=0,\dots,N-1, \end{align*} then the solution \eqref{E:mkdet} becomes \begin{align*} \det M_k =& f_k \left(1+g_k \sum_{i=0}^{k} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k} y_i, \end{align*} and \eqref{E:mndet} becomes \begin{align*} \det M_N =& \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2} \prod_{i=0}^{N-1} y_i. \end{align*} Substituting \eqref{E:mkdet} in the RHS of \eqref{E:mrecursion} we get that for $k=2,\dots,N$ \begin{align*} & \alpha_k \det M_{k-1} - \beta_k \det M_{k-2}\\ &= \alpha_k f_{k-1} \left(1+g_{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{k-1} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i - \beta_k f_{k-2}\left(1+g_{k-2}\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i \right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-2} y_i\\ &= \left( \alpha_k f_{k-1} \left(1+g_{k-1} x_{k-1}+g_{k-1}\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i\right)-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2}-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} g_{k-2}\sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i \right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i\\ &= \left( \alpha_k f_{k-1}(1+ g_{k-1} x_{k-1}) -\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2}+\left( \alpha_k f_{k-1} g_{k-1}-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} g_{k-2}\right) \sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i. \end{align*} It is straightforward (although somewhat involved) to verify that for $k<N$ \begin{align*} & \alpha_k f_{k-1} (1+ g_{k-1} x_{k-1}) -\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} = f_k y_k (1+g_k x_{k-1}+g_k x_k), \end{align*} and \begin{align*} & \alpha_k f_{k-1}g_{k-1}-\frac{\beta_k}{y_{k-1}} f_{k-2} g_{k-2} = f_k g_k y_k. \end{align*} We therefore get \begin{align*} & \alpha_k \det M_{k-1} -\beta_k \det M_{k-2} \\ & = \left( f_k y_k(1+g_k x_{k-1}+g_k x_k)+ f_k g_k y_k \sum_{i=0}^{k-2} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k-1} y_i\\ & = f_k \left( 1+g_k \sum_{i=0}^{k} x_i\right) \prod_{i=0}^{k} y_i\\ & = \det M_k, \end{align*} and thus \eqref{E:mkdet} satisfies \eqref{E:mrecursion}. It is also possible to show that \begin{align*} & \alpha_N f_{N-1}(1+ g_{N-1} x_{N-1}) -\frac{\beta_N}{y_{N-1}} f_{N-2} = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2}, \\ & \alpha_N f_{N-1} g_{N-1}-\frac{\beta_N}{y_{N-1}} f_{N-2} g_{N-2} = 0, \end{align*} thus, for $k=N$ \begin{align*} & \alpha_N \det M_{N-1} -\beta_N \det M_{N-2} \\ & = \frac{(2N+1)^2}{(N+1)^2} \prod_{i=0}^{N-1} y_i \\ & = \det M_N, \end{align*} and the expression \eqref{E:mndet} is also verified.
nodes.statement_short: Check the base cases and that the closed forms satisfy the recursion, via the auxiliary quantities $\alpha_k,\beta_k,f_i,g_i,x_i,y_i$.
nodes.section: A Proof of Lemma 3.3

nodes.name: Conclude positivity of all minors
nodes.statement: To complete the proof, note that the closed form expressions for $\det M_k$ consist of sums and products of positive values, hence $\det M_k$ is positive, and thus follows from Sylvester's criterion that $S_1$ is positive definite.
nodes.statement_short: All minors are sums and products of positive numbers, so Sylvester's criterion applies.
